title: Idiomatic expressions
why: This lesson closes the unit on culture and leisure with a dozen idioms you'll hear every day in France, from avoir le cafard to poser un lapin. You learn their literal image, their real meaning and their English equivalent, and how to use them in the right register.
json:
{"lessons": ["

Moods and energy

Idioms are the spice of everyday French. You'll hear them all the time among friends and colleagues, and using one at the right moment makes you sound instantly more natural. The trick: never translate them word for word. Learn each one with its literal meaning (it helps you remember) and its real meaning.

ExpressionLiterallyMeaning
avoir le cafardto have the cockroachto feel down, to have the blues
avoir un coup de barreto get a blow from the barto suddenly feel exhausted, to hit a wall
avoir la flemmeto have the lazinessto not be bothered, to feel too lazy
faire la grasse matinéeto do the fat morningto sleep in
avoir la tête dans les nuagesto have your head in the cloudsthe same as in English: to be daydreaming

These are normal verb phrases: conjugate avoir and faire in any tense. Avoir la flemme takes de + infinitive, like avoir envie de.

J'ai la flemme de faire la vaisselle.I can't be bothered to do the dishes.
Dimanche, on a fait la grasse matinée jusqu'à midi.On Sunday, we slept in until noon.
Après le déjeuner, j'ai toujours un coup de barre.After lunch, I always hit a wall.

These expressions are informal: perfect with friends, family and most colleagues, but avoid them in a formal email. To a client, say je suis très fatigué, not j'ai un coup de barre.

", "

People and situations

ExpressionLiterallyMeaning
poser un lapin à quelqu'unto put down a rabbit for someoneto stand someone up
donner un coup de main à quelqu'unto give someone a blow of the handto give someone a hand
mettre les pieds dans le platto put your feet in the dishto put your foot in it
appeler un chat un chatto call a cat a catto call a spade a spade

Watch the pronouns: poser un lapin and donner un coup de main are built with à quelqu'un, so they take indirect pronouns, me, te, lui, nous, vous, leur:

Julien m'a posé un lapin. Il lui a posé un lapin.Julien stood me up. He stood her up.
Tu peux me donner un coup de main samedi ?Can you give me a hand on Saturday?
Je ne savais pas qu'ils étaient séparés : j'ai mis les pieds dans le plat !I didn't know they had split up: I put my foot in it!
Avec Camille, pas de détour : elle appelle un chat un chat.With Camille, no beating around the bush: she calls a spade a spade.

Notice how close some are to English (a hand, a foot), and how others use a completely different image (a rabbit!). The close ones are easy wins; the different ones are worth a little extra practice.

Mettre les pieds dans le plat is about a social blunder: saying the wrong thing at the wrong moment. For a simple mistake, just say je me suis trompé(e).

", "

Price and difficulty

ExpressionLiterallyMeaning
coûter les yeux de la têteto cost the eyes of the headto cost an arm and a leg
c'est du gâteauit's cakeit's a piece of cake
ce n'est pas la mer à boireit's not the sea to drinkit's not that hard, it's no big deal
Les appartements à Paris coûtent les yeux de la tête.Apartments in Paris cost an arm and a leg.
— Tu as réussi l'examen ? — Oui, c'était du gâteau !— Did you pass the exam? — Yes, it was a piece of cake!
Ne t'inquiète pas, ce n'est pas la mer à boire.Don't worry, it's not that hard.

Using idioms well

  • Use them in the right situation: one well-placed idiom is better than five in a row.
  • Keep the words exactly as they are: les yeux de la tête, never \"les yeux de ma tête\".
  • Don't translate English idioms into French: \"it's raining cats and dogs\" means nothing in French, where it rains ropes, il pleut des cordes.

In speech, ce n'est pas la mer à boire often becomes c'est pas la mer à boire, but in writing keep the full negation.

A good way to remember them: picture the literal image. A rabbit waiting alone at a café, someone drinking the whole sea, a price tag asking for your eyes!
